It is the classical {\it weak keeper\/} ,
{\it staticizer\/} , {\it bleeder\/}
of the {\tt TSPC} $\div 2$.

$$D= \bar Q\;\;{\rm so}\;\;Q_{n+1}= \bar Q_{n}$$

with master made of $TG_{1}+{\rm Inv}_{1}$
and slave $TG_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{2}+{\rm Inv}_{3}$
closed in a ring is normally {\it all dynamic}.

In the ideal $CK/\bar {CK}$ non overlap case
with $C_{gs}$ alone:

* $CK=1\;,\;\bar {CK}=0$ : $Y=X$, $Z=\bar Y$,
$W=$ floating, $V=\bar W$, $X=\bar V$ holds

* $CK=0\;,\;\bar {CK}=1$ : $Y=$ floating, $Z=\bar Y$
holds, $W=Z$, $V=\bar W$, $X=\bar V=Z$ copied

so on every $0\to 1\to 0$ {\it full} period

$$Z_{n+1}= \bar Z_{n}\qquad X_{n+1}= \bar X_{n}$$

$\div 2$ only so long as the charge on the
floating node, $Y$ in $\Phi_{1}=0$ and $W$ in
$\Phi_{1}=1$, does not leak away. In normal
CMOS

$$\tau _{leak}\approx C_{node}V_{DD}/I_{leak}\approx
10^{-13}/10^{-9}\approx 10^{-4} {\rm s}$$

so

$$f_{min}\approx 10^{4}-10^{6}{\rm Hz},\;\;
f_{max}\approx 1/3t_{p}$$

any stop of the clock, any slow clock, any
coupling noise, clock feed through, charge
sharing on $Y,W$ destroys the state. It is
normally called {\it dynamic\/} and {\it
ratioless\/}:

$$P_{dyn}=C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f\;\;,\;\;t_{CQ}=t_{TG}+t_{Inv}$$
minimum.

Putting the red ${\rm Inv}$ in the master, in
sign as a {\it cross coupled latch} with
${\rm Inv}_{1}$

$$Y \xrightarrow{{\rm Inv}_{1}} Z
 \xrightarrow{{\rm red}}X \xrightarrow{TG_{1}}Y$$

in the drawing as a {\it parallel} driver
$$X\;\xrightarrow[{\rm red}]{{\rm Inv}_{1}}\;Z$$
it is the same thing {\it modulo} $TG_{1}$,
makes the master {\it pseudo static}, {\it
ratioed}.

In the transparent phase, $CK=1$, the two
${\rm Inv}$ drive $Z$ in {\it parallel}, {\it
a fortiori} faster. In the hold phase,
$CK=0$, $\bar {CK}=1$,

$$Z =\bar Y\;\;{\rm from\;Inv}_{1}\;\;{\rm with\;\;}
Y=Q_{n}={\rm floating\;capacitor}$$

is now held by

$$Z =\bar X\;\;{\rm from\;red\;\;with\;\;}
X= W = Z\;\;{\rm from\;slave}$$

{\it i. e.} the red ${\rm Inv}$ fights
${\rm Inv}_{1}$ on $Z$, or, if you draw it as
$Z\to X$, it fights the slave on $X$.

So for DC:

* Pro: the loop gain $>1$ holds $Y/Z$
for $f\to 0$. No $f_{min}$. The node is
low impedance, restored to $V_{DD}/V_{SS}$,
noise margin goes from $\approx 0$ dynamic
to $NM_{H,L}\approx V_{DD}/3$, clock feed
through and leakage insensitive, rail to
rail, can be stopped. In modern jargon the
conventional TSPC becomes the E-TSPC,
extended TSPC, and can even be made faster
because the series ${\rm MOS}$ in the
clocked ${\rm Inv}$ can be suppressed.

* Contra: ratioed logic. During the {\it
write} the driver must over power the keeper.

For the master to be writable

$$ \left({W\over L}\right)_{red}<<
   \left({W\over L}\right)_{Inv_{1}},
   \left({W\over L}\right)_{slave}$$

normally $1/3$ to $1/10$ and long $L$,
high $V_{t}$ if possible.  If that ratio is
not respected the latch cannot be flipped,
the divider is stuck, $Q_{n+1}=Q_{n}$, it
does not $\div 2$.

Even correctly ratioed:

* added $C_{g}+C_{d}$ on $X,Y,Z$, about
$20-30\%$ extra fan out, so

$$t_{CQ}^{stat}=t_{CQ}^{dyn}+ \Delta t_{red}
  +t_{fight}\approx 1.1-1.5\,t_{CQ}^{dyn}$$

$$f_{max}^{stat}\approx 0.7-0.9\,f_{max}^{dyn}$$

in $0.18\mu$ e. {\it g.} $5.0{\rm GHz}
\to 3.5-4.5{\rm GHz}$.

* a direct $V_{DD}\to V_{SS}$ short circuit
current during the fight

$$I_{sc}\approx {1\over 2}\mu C_{ox}{W\over L}
 \left(V_{DD}-V_{t}\right)^{2}\;\;{\rm for}\;\;
  t_{sc}\approx t_{r,f}$$

so

$$P =C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f +V_{DD}I_{sc}t_{sc}f$$

$10-30\%$ more power, static power
$\ne 0$ during transition, $PDP$ worse.

* $t_{setup},t_{hold}$ of the equivalent
$D\,{\rm FF}$ are degraded, essentially the
hold time must cover the fight time.

* process, $V_{DD}$, $T$ variation of the
ratio can make it fail at low $V_{DD}$ or
high $T$.

In one sentence: you buy DC, leakage and
noise robustness and rail to rail operation
for area, for a small to large, depending on
sizing, loss in $t_{p}$, $f_{max}$ and
$P_{dyn}+P_{sc}$ and you make the circuit
ratioed. Made weak enough it is a negligible
penalty, made as strong as ${\rm Inv}_{1}$
it kills the divider.

> {\it Remark:} In the literature the weak
> red ${\rm Inv}$ is normally gated with a
> $TG_{2}$ so that it is disconnected during
> the write, {\it e. g.} the conventional
> $TG$ static master-slave $D\,{\rm FF}$,
> to suppress the $I_{sc}$.  Unclocked as
> drawn it is the E-TSPC $\div 2$.

answer.text:
Without the inverter in red the loop is dynamic.

* `CK=1` : $Y = X$, $Z = \bar Y$, $\overline{CK}=0$ and
$D$ floats.
* `CK=0` : $Y$ floats, $Z = \bar Y$, $D = Z$,
$Q = \bar{\bar D} = Z$.

With $Q$ fed back to $X$, $Q_{new} = \bar Q_{old}$.
It is a toggle master-slave, a $\div 2$.

$Y$ on master-hold and $D$ on slave-hold are stored
only on gate capacitance. The circuit can be very fast
because there is no fight and minimum capacitance in
the loop, but it fails at low clock rate from leakage,
noise, clock feedthrough.

$Inv_{1}$ plus the red inverter is a back-to-back
keeper for the master latch:

```
Y ---Inv1---> Z
Y <--red----- Z
```

On hold, $CK=0$, it holds $Y,Z$ statically.
On sample, $CK=1$, it is in parallel aiding.

Logically nothing changes, but for timing/power:

1. **Load in the signal path.** $Inv_{1}$ in sampling
mode must now drive the $\overline{CK}$ switch
capacitance *plus* $C_{in}$ of the red inverter.
Its $Y\to Z$ delay, which is directly in the
toggle loop delay $t_{loop}$, goes up.

$t_{loop}\approx t_{CK}+t_{Inv1}+t_{\overline{CK}}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}$

$f_{max} \approx 1/2t_{loop}$ goes down.

2. **Contention on write.** On a new sample the
data coming through the $CK$ switch to $Y$ must
overpower the keeper trying to hold the old $Y$.
The write becomes ratioed. That means:

* slower $X\to Y$ transition,
* crowbar current while input fights keeper,
* you must upsize the sampling switch and the
driving stage, i.e. more clock load, more area,
more $CV^{2}$ power.

In short you buy static, down-to-DC, more robust
operation with lower $f_{max}$ and higher power.

That is why the keeper is made weak, minimum $W/L$,
just strong enough to beat leakage, and why
very high speed dividers often omit it and stay
dynamic, accepting a minimum operating frequency.

answer.text:
This is a toggle flip-flop - a master-slave wired
divide-by-2.

* CK on : SW1 on, SW2 off. Master transparent,
  slave in hold.
  `A -> B -> C = ~B`, `D` floating, `F = Dold = Aold`
* CKbar on : SW1 off, SW2 on. Master in hold,
  slave transparent.
  `B` floating, `C = ~B`, `D = C -> E = ~D -> F = D`

so on 1->0 `F=A` goes to `~Aold`. Without the
red device it is dynamic: `B` floats with SW1
off, `D` floats with SW2 off.

A static keeper for the master is back-to-back
around `Inv1`, i.e. from `C` to `B`, the
internal node after SW1. That is not where the
red inverter is.

As drawn it goes from `C` to `A`, the input
side of SW1. That:

1. does not make anything static. `B`, the node
that actually floats, is still floating. `A`
is always driven by `Inv3`.

2. just loads the forward path. The input capacitance
of the red inverter is extra load on `C`, output
of `Inv1`, and its output capacitance is extra
load on `A`. Master evaluation:

```
tB-C ~ R_Inv1 * (C_SW2 + C_Inv2 + C_red,in)
```

goes up, setup and clk-to-Q go up, `fmax` for
the divider goes down.

3. puts ratioed contention in the loop.

Take the red as pointing left, `C -> A`, like
a normal back-to-back.

CK = 1, master transparent: `B = A`, `C = ~A`.
Red wants `A = ~C = A`. OK.

CK = 0, slave transparent: Master holds `C = ~Aold`.
Slave wants:

```
D = C = ~Aold
F = D = ~Aold
A = F = ~Aold
```

Red wants:

```
A = ~C = Aold
```

i.e. `Inv3` and red fight directly on `A` for
the whole half cycle. To toggle, the slave must
overpower the red inverter. You get:

* much slower falling transition of `A/F`,
  much larger clk-to-Q
* static crowbar current for half a period
* ratioed operation. If red is strong the
  divider fails to toggle.

In fact during CKbar-on you have closed:

```
C -> SW2 -> Inv2 -> Inv3 -> A -> red -> C
```

That is 3 inversions in a loop - a ring oscillator.
Instead of holding, the circuit wants to oscillate.

In short: misplaced keeper gives no low-frequency
hold benefit, and costs speed, power and robustness.
For high speed remove it and stay dynamic. For
static operation move it to `C -> B` and make it
weak so `Inv1` and the driver can easily overpower
it when transparent.

answer.text:
This is a master-slave $D=Q$ divider.

* Let $D$ = left of the $CK$ switch = divider input = divider output
* $X$ = right of $CK$ switch = input of ${\rm Inv_{1}}$
* $Y$ = output of ${\rm Inv_{1}}$ = left of $\overline{CK}$ switch
* $S$ = right of $\overline{CK}$ switch

Without color the path is:

$$D \xrightarrow{CK} X \xrightarrow{{\rm Inv1}} Y
  \xrightarrow{\overline{CK}} S \xrightarrow{{\rm Inv2}}
  \xrightarrow{{\rm Inv3}} Q = D$$

3 inversions $D$ to $Q$, so $Q=\overline{D}$ : toggle.

Without the red device it is fully dynamic and ratio-less.
When $CK=1$, $X=D$, $Y=\bar D$, $S$ floats.
When $CK=0$, $X$ floats, $Y=\bar X$, $S=Y$, $Q=Y$.
$X$ and $S$ are stored on gate capacitance. Fast,
no static current, but fails at low clock rate.

You want to staticize the master with a local
weak feedback $Y \to X$. The red inverter is put
$Y \to D$ instead, i.e. output of ${\rm Inv_{1}}$
back to the divider input.

That is a global feedback fighting the divider output driver.

Put $Y$ = input of red, $D$ = output of red.

* $CK=1:$ master transparent, slave hold.

$$X=D,\quad Y=\bar D$$

Red drives $D=\bar Y = D$. Same as $Q$ drives
$D$. No DC fight, just extra load.

* $CK=0:$ master hold, slave transparent.

$$X = X_{prev},\quad Y=\bar X_{prev}$$
$$S=Y,\quad Q=Y\;{\rm after\;2\;inv},\quad D=Q=Y$$

Red drives $D=\bar Y$.

i.e. the final output inverter drives $D=Y$
and the red inverter drives $D=\bar Y$ continuously.

So for half the cycle the two inverters fight at node $D$.

Consequences:

1. **Ratioed logic.** To toggle, $Q$ must overpower red.
Red must be made very weak, $Q$-driver very strong.
If red is too strong the divider sticks and does not
divide.

2. **Static power.** For essentially the whole $CK=0$
phase there is a direct $V_{DD}$ to $GND$ current
through the fighting PMOS/NMOS of $Q$-driver and red.

3. **Speed loss.** The fight has to be won on every
$CK$ falling edge when $Q$ must flip $D$ to the new
value. The $CK$-to-$Q$ delay is increased by the contention.
In addition red loads $Y$, the high speed master output,
with gate capacitance, and loads $D$ with drain
capacitance. Both increase loop delay and lower $f_{max}$.
Dynamic $CV^{2}f$ power is also increased.

4. **No static benefit.** The dynamic nodes remain dynamic.
$X$ floats when $CK=0$, $S$ floats when $CK=1$.
Red does not close a $Y\to X$ latch, it closes a
$D\to Y\to S\to Q\to D$ odd-inversion loop fighting
${\rm Inv_{1}}$/$Q$. It does not hold $X$ or $S$ against leakage.
Low-frequency failure is not cured.

In short: slower edges, lower maximum divide frequency,
static plus larger dynamic power, larger area for ratioing,
worse robustness, with no hold improvement.

The correct staticizer is a weak $Y\to X$ local inverter.
Then the fight is only between the $CK$ sampling device
and a weak keeper during write, not between two
active inverters during hold.

The circuit is a dynamic master–slave divide-by-two. Let

- $Q$ be the node at the far left (the output of the last black inverter, fed back to the input), and
- $X$ be the output of $\text{Inv}_1$.

The red inverter is an **unclocked feed-forward inverter in parallel with the clocked master latch** ($\text{CK}$ switch $+\ \text{Inv}_1$). It is not a keeper: a keeper would feed $X$ back to the input of $\text{Inv}_1$, whereas this device feeds $Q$ forward to $X$ at all times.

**When $CK$ is on ($\overline{CK}$ off)** the master is transparent and the slave holds $Q$. The input of $\text{Inv}_1$ is then $Q$ (through the closed switch), so the red inverter and $\text{Inv}_1$ do exactly the same job, in parallel:

$$X=\bar Q .$$

Two things help speed. First, the red path bypasses the series resistance of the $\text{CK}$ switch, so $X$ starts moving as soon as $Q$ moves instead of waiting for the input node of $\text{Inv}_1$ to charge through the switch. Second, once $\text{Inv}_1$ turns on, two inverters drive the capacitance at $X$ instead of one. The master therefore settles in well under a half clock period, and the maximum toggle frequency of the divider goes up. In fact the red inverter even starts pre-driving $X$ toward its *next* value during the preceding $\overline{CK}$ phase, so part of the master delay is hidden.

**When $CK$ is off ($\overline{CK}$ on)** the master is supposed to be in hold and completely isolated from the slave. $\text{Inv}_1$ holds $X=\bar Q_{\text{old}}$ from the charge stored on its input node, the slave makes $Q_{\text{new}}=X=\bar Q_{\text{old}}$, and the divider has toggled. But the red inverter is still connected, and it now *disagrees* with $\text{Inv}_1$:

$$\text{Inv}_1:\; X=\bar Q_{\text{old}}=Q_{\text{new}},\qquad 
\text{red}:\; X=\bar Q_{\text{new}}=Q_{\text{old}} .$$

So during the whole hold phase the red inverter fights $\text{Inv}_1$ for node $X$: there is contention (crowbar) current, the swing and noise margin at $X$ are degraded, and the red device’s gate capacitance loads $Q$ while its drain capacitance loads $X$, slowing the slave a little and raising power. Worse, $X\!\to\!$Inv$_2\!\to\!$Inv$_3\!\to\!Q\!\to\!$red$\!\to\!X$ is a closed loop of three inverters. If the $\overline{CK}$ phase lasts longer than the delay around that loop, $X$ is dragged across the slave’s threshold, $Q$ flips back, then flips again — the loop ring-oscillates and the $\div2$ action is lost. Correct operation at high speed relies on the clock phase ending before that unwanted second toggle gets around the loop.

**Net effect:** the operating window is shifted *up* in frequency. $f_{\max}$ increases (the reason the device is added in RF prescalers, where the clock is always present and fast), but a substantial $f_{\min}$ appears, well above the leakage-limited minimum of the plain dynamic divider: the circuit misbehaves at low clock rates, oscillates if the clock stops with $CK$ low, and burns extra power in contention. The red inverter is therefore sized as a compromise — strong enough to start $X$ swinging quickly, weak/delayed enough not to overpower $\text{Inv}_1$ and corrupt $X$ within one half-cycle.

The state is held, in alternate clock phases, as charge on
the input capacitance of ${\rm Inv}_1$ and on the input
capacitance of the following inverter.  It therefore has a
minimum clock frequency set by leakage.

The red inverter is meant to be the back-to-back keeper
for ${\rm Inv}_1$, but as drawn it is not connected directly
across ${\rm Inv}_1$: its loop contains the $CK$ switch.

* $CK$ off, $\overline{CK}$ on: this is the phase in which
the input node of ${\rm Inv}_1$ is floating and needs to be
held.  The $CK$ switch is open, so the keeper loop is open.
That node still floats and still leaks.  The circuit is not
made static, and $f_{\min }$ and clock-stop behaviour are
unchanged.

* $CK$ on: the keeper loop is closed, but the input of
${\rm Inv}_1$ is then already driven through $CK$ by the
recirculating signal.  The keeper is redundant.

Worse, in the $\overline{CK}$ phase the output of the red
inverter is tied to the recirculating node.  When the right
hand inverters try to toggle that node to its new value,
the red inverter, fed from the old output of ${\rm Inv}_1$,
tries to hold it at its old value.  The right-most inverter
must overpower the red inverter on every toggle.  The red
inverter also loads the output of ${\rm Inv}_1$ and the
recirculating node.

Hence, as drawn, the red inverter gives no static-holding
benefit, but increases clock-to-output delay and contention
power, lowers $f_{\max }$, and, if it is not much weaker than
the right-most inverter, can prevent the circuit from
toggling at all.  A useful keeper must be connected directly
across ${\rm Inv}_1$, on the ${\rm Inv}_1$ side of the $CK$
switch, and made deliberately weak.

The black circuit is a dynamic toggle flip-flop. The values at
the inputs of the inverters are stored only on gate capacitance
while $CK$ or $\overline{CK}$ is off, so it will not retain its
state for a long, or stopped, clock period.

${\rm Inv_1}$.  It cross-couples the first stage:

* it regeneratively holds the state of ${\rm Inv_1}$, so leakage
at the dynamic node no longer destroys the stored bit.  In
principle the stage now works down to dc, with much better
immunity to leakage and noise.

* on every change of state the new value must fight the keeper.
The driver, here the last inverter through the $CK$ switch,
must overpower the red inverter, and the red inverter loads
the output of ${\rm Inv_1}$.

Hence retention is gained at the expense of speed and power:
larger clock-to-output delay, contention current during
switching, increased power, and a lower maximum toggle
frequency.  The red inverter must therefore be made very weak
-- small $W/L$, long channel -- compared with ${\rm Inv_1}$ and
with the inverter driving it.  Made full strength, it will
seriously slow, and can even prevent, the divide-by-two
action.

answer.text:
The red gate is not an additional stage in the loop – it is the same kind of inverter as Inv1 but wired in parallel with it:

• Its input is tied to the same node that feeds Inv1.  
• Its output is shorted to the output of Inv1.  

Electrically this is equivalent to making the first stage of the ring oscillator twice as wide.

What changes?

1. Delay of the first stage  
   – Two identical pull-up/pull-down devices in parallel give one-half of the effective on-resistance, so the intrinsic delay of that stage is roughly cut in half.

2. Load seen by the preceding stage  
   – The input capacitance doubles, so the node that drives CK now has to charge/discharge twice the gate-capacitance. That stretches the delay of the preceding stage.

3. Net effect on the oscillation period  
   – In practice the reduction in the first-stage delay is usually larger than the increase in the previous-stage delay, so the loop oscillates a little faster. (How much faster depends on sizing; if the preceding stage is already weak the gain can disappear or even turn into a loss.)

4. Power and area  
   – About twice the silicon area for that stage and roughly twice the dynamic power associated with switching it (because two gate/input caps and two output nodes are being charged and discharged every cycle).

5. Reliability/glitch behaviour  
   – Because both inverters have the same input, their outputs are always intended to be the same logic level. During a transition they may not switch at exactly the same instant, so for a few picoseconds they can fight each other, giving a small increase in short-circuit current, but this is normally harmless.

In short, the red inverter is a straightforward way of strengthening (widening) the first stage. It can increase the ring-oscillator frequency or shorten a critical path at the cost of more load on the previous node, higher power and larger area.

answer.text:
The red inverter is the so-called keeper (or feedback) inverter that is normally added to a dynamic / domino gate.

What it does  
1. Noise-/leakage hold:  
   • During the pre-charge phase (CK = 0, CK-bar = 1) the dynamic node in front of Inv1 is charged to VDD.  
   • When the clock stays low, the node would otherwise be a high-impedance capacitor and could be disturbed by leakage, charge sharing, α-particle hits, etc.  
   • The keeper senses the high level at the output of Inv1 and feeds a weak pull-up back to the dynamic node, so the node is “latched” high and cannot drift.

2. Turns the domino gate into a pseudo-static gate:  
   Even if the circuit is stopped for an arbitrarily long time in the evaluation phase, the output will not lose its state thanks to the keeper.

How it affects performance

Delay:  
• When the evaluation network wants to discharge the dynamic node (logic 1 → 0 transition) it first has to fight the keeper’s pull-up device.  
• This contention current and the extra gate/drain capacitance of the keeper slow the falling transition of the dynamic node, so the high-to-low delay of the stage increases.  
• Rising transitions (0 → 1) are almost unaffected because the pre-charge PMOS overrides the keeper.

Power:  
• Extra short-circuit (crowbar) current flows for a few hundred picoseconds each time the dynamic node is pulled low because both the keeper PMOS and the evaluation NMOS stack are momentarily ON.  
• Additional dynamic power is consumed to charge / discharge the keeper’s gate capacitance every clock cycle.

Sizing trade-off  
• A strong keeper gives excellent noise immunity but produces large contention and therefore large delay and power.  
• A very weak keeper minimises delay/power but may not be able to hold the node reliably at low clock frequencies or under noise.  
• In practice the keeper is made just strong enough (W/L ≈ 1/4-1/10 of the evaluation pull-down strength).

In short:  
The red inverter greatly improves robustness by keeping the pre-charged node from floating, but it slows down the evaluation transition and adds some static/dynamic power. The designer sizes it to balance speed and noise immunity.

answer.text:
The red gate is nothing more than a “keeper” (or feedback) inverter.  
Together with the clock-controlled inverter Inv1 it forms a two-inverter
loop, i.e. a small static latch.  
Its presence changes the circuit from a purely dynamic latch (or
sample-and-hold) into a static one that can keep its logic level for an
unlimited time.

What it gives you  
1. Static data retention – the stored value does not leak away when CK is
   low because the cross-coupled pair regenerates the level.  
2. Full noise margin – the node in front of Inv1 is driven to a legal rail
   voltage instead of being left floating.  
3. Practically zero hold-time requirement – as soon as CK falls, the keeper
   takes over and the data at the latch input may change.

What it costs you  
1. Extra capacitive load – the input capacitance of the red inverter is
   added to the output node of Inv1 and its output capacitance is added to
   the sampling node.  
2. Fight/contending drivers when CK rises – while the input tries to drive
   the sampling node, the red inverter is still driving the previous value
   for a few tens of picoseconds.  The input must overcome this, so
      • D-to-Q (or CK-to-Q) delay increases,  
      • the required set-up time increases.  
3. Some additional dynamic and short-circuit power and a little more area.

In short  

• Without the red inverter – smallest and fastest, but only a dynamic
  latch (cannot stop the clock, poor noise margin, data fades with leakage).  

• With the red inverter – robust, static storage and relaxed hold-time, but
  propagation delay and set-up time are a little worse and power/area are
  slightly higher.

So the red inverter improves reliability and low-frequency operation at the
expense of peak-speed performance.

- **Reduced speed / oscillation frequency.** Inv₁'s gate capacitance loads the feedback node (output of the last inverter) and its output capacitance loads the node between the first inverter and the CK̄ switch.
